rejected_videos.reason: Entire video is a deep-dive into the mutable-default-argument gotcha, explicitly framed as a follow-up to 'my last video on five common python mistakes' (an unresolved earlier-context reference). It never states or demonstrates this concept's required facts: basic default-parameter syntax (f1), calling with keyword arguments (f2), or the keyword-argument matching/uniqueness rule (f3). No clean sub-range teaches the required facts without the advanced gotcha framing.

Video is a z-score/IQR outlier-detection coding tutorial. The brief outlier definition (~59-104s) is immediately followed by percentile and z-score math and Python code that require untaught prerequisites (standard deviation, percentiles) -- requires untaught knowledge. It never states that examining outliers reveals skew/errors/interesting properties (f2) or that a genuine outlier should not be removed without good reason (f3); it only frames outliers as things to detect and exclude mathematically. No clean segment isolates the required facts from the advanced math.

Video (part 4 of a pandas series) opens with an unresolved reference to 'the previous tutorial' and is entirely about customizing a matplotlib heatmap of an already-computed correlation table plus web-scraping state abbreviations -- it never discusses judging correlation strength by magnitude regardless of sign (f1) or confounding variables (f2). Wrong content for this concept.

Assumes the datetime conversion already happened off-screen ('it is this guy, it's apparently date time now' -- unresolved earlier context from a prior, unshown step) and never shows a to_datetime() call (f1). The year/month/day/hour extraction is described only vaguely ('I write this line... creates one that is only date') without ever naming the .dt accessor or showing its syntax in the transcript, so f2 isn't clearly taught either. The rest of the video drifts into filtering bad data and prepping for a model -- off-topic for this concept.

Video is a tour of specific Excel functions (MAX/MIN, IF, LEN, LEFT/RIGHT, CONCATENATE, SUM, COUNT, etc.); it never explains reference notation itself -- A1-style cell addresses, A10:A20 range syntax, or whole-row/column references like 5:5 or H:H are never stated out loud. Ranges are selected by clicking/dragging on screen without narrating the notation, so the required facts aren't taught.

Video teaches multi-panel layout via fig.add_subplot(nrows, ncols, index) and plt.subplot2grid() with rowspan/colspan, not the specific APIs this concept names: plt.subplots(2, 2) (f1) or plt.subplot(131)/plt.subplot(132)/plt.subplot(133) with plt.suptitle() (f2). plt.suptitle() is never mentioned, and the three-digit plt.subplot() shorthand is never used (only the object-oriented fig.add_subplot(2,1,1) form, and a separate plt.subplot2grid() API). Teaching a different, unrelated API would not satisfy facts that specifically describe this function/syntax.
